READING PASSAGE 1
You should spend about 20 minutes on Questions 1-13, which are based on Reading Passage 1
on pages 2 and 3.
The Changing Nature of Selling
Technology is having a dramatic impact on sales techniques
The nature of selling is undergoing
a transformation, argues author
Daniel Pink. The salesperson of the
past is becoming an endangered
species in a new sales environment.
Pink maintains that all of us are
increasingly in the business of sales
in one way or another, whether we
realise it or not. Doctors selling
remedies to patients, lawyers
bringing juries around to a verdict,
and coaches motivating their
players - all are in the sales game.
Pink argues that traditionally in
Western society there’s been an
attitude that salespeople are
untrustworthy or even dishonest.
But the sales techniques
responsible for this — those
practised by the traditional fast-
talking salesman — tell us more
about the conditions in which sales
have long taken place, rather than
the nature of sales itself. ‘When
sellers have more information than
buyers,’ he says, ‘sellers can
hoodwink you, they can rip you off.’
But now the information imbalance
that defined much of the sales
relationship is changing. And that’s
largely thanks to the internet, and
the fact that buyers have immediate
access to information about
products.
In the United States about one
in nine people work in sales, a
figure that has remained
unchanged over the past decade
despite the technology revolution.
But according to Pink we are
engaged in selling in its broadest
sense whenever we attempt to
persuade, convince or influence
others. Studying his diary one day,
Pink categorised how his days had
been divided up. He found most of
his time had been spent trying to
persuade someone to do something
— whether pitching ideas, asking a
potential business partner to join
forces, or urging an organisation
where he did voluntary work to
shift strategies. In a survey Pink
commissioned of 9,000
respondents, he found people
spend about 40% of their time at
work engaged in persuasion - in
other words influencing and
convincing others in ways that
don’t involve a purchase. People
said they considered this aspect of
their work crucial to their
professional success.
At some organisations this wider
interpretation of sales is already
understood. One such outfit is
software firm Atlassian, whose
customers include multinational
corporations. Yet Atlassian has no
dedicated ‘sales department’.
Instead, all employees are
considered to be salespeople, by
being expected to meet customer
needs and having to understand
how the company’s products will be
used.
Although the old idea behind
sales was ABC - Always Be Closing

— (meaning always make a deal) -
Pink maintains that today sales
require a new ABC approach:
Attunement, Buoyancy and Clarity.
‘Attunement’ is about tuning in to
another person’s view of the world,
so you can better respond to what
he or she wants. This isn’t the same
as empathy, says Pink, which is
about understanding someone
else’s emotions. Instead, it requires
getting inside someone else’s brain
to understand what he or she is
thinking. One technique that seems
to promote attunement is physical
imitation. According to Pink, there’s
a lot of evidence that subtly
repeating someone’s gestures,
which is something human beings
do naturally, can enhance your
powers of attunement.
A Dutch study found that
waiters in a restaurant who read
back diners’ orders word for word
earned 70% more tips than those
who paraphrased them. The diners
were also most satisfied with their
dining experience, a result
researchers put down to the waiters
having been seen to attune with
their customers. A lack of
attunement is the key to one of the
most surprising findings of Pink’s
research: that extroverts are not
good salespeople. The reason
extroverts perform poorly is they
talk too much and overwhelm the
person they are talking to. They
don’t spend time listening, so they
never attune.
Perhaps the most valuable trait
to cultivate in the new ABC is
‘buoyancy’, the ability to bounce
back after rejection. This is often
seen as completely determined by
personality but in fact it can be
learnt, says Pink, even by people
who are generally quite negative.
Before an important meeting, the
traditional approach has been to
build self-confidence by saying 1
can do it’. Wrong, says Pink.
Instead of telling yourself I can do
it’, it’s better to ask yourself, ‘Can I
do it?’, because asking questions
allows you to think about and
pinpoint the actual strategies
necessary to do the job well, rather
than just feeling good about it. And
for maintaining buoyancy after a
rejection, Pink points to studies at
the University of Pennsylvania.
Researchers found that people who
give up easily tend to think that
they themselves are the cause of
bad events, while buoyant
personalities are less likely to blame
themselves. In other words, the
explanation someone uses when
reflecting on a negative event is
crucial to how optimistic they feel
about the future.
The third quality needed is
‘clarity’. Pink gives the example of a
top confectionery company whose
salespeople now have a
brainstorming session with
shopkeepers on maximising sales —
even if it means suggesting the
customer buys products made by a
competitor — if it will improve the
shopkeeper’s knowledge of the
confectionery business. In one
sense, concludes Pink, we are
seeing the death of the traditional
salesman. But he argues we are
also seeing the rebirth of the need
for selling, but of a different nature.

Questions 1-6
Do the following statements agree with the information given in Reading Passage 1?
In boxes 1-6 on your answer sheet, write
TRUE if the statement agrees with the information
FALSE if the statement contradicts the information
NOT GIVEN if there is no information on this
1 Traditionally, Western society has had little respect for salespeople.
2 The techniques used by ‘fast-talking’ salesmen were difficult to learn.
3 The relationship between sellers and buyers was more equal in the past than it is
today.
4 In the US, fewer people work in sales today than ten years ago.
5 A survey of 9,000 people found that respondents recognised the significance of
persuasion in their jobs.
6 Atlassian has one specific group of staff responsible for sales.
